To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

mixed grazing systems incorporating both cattle and sheep, and semi natural rough grazing, benefit both upland livestock production and biodiversity, but that there is little evidence that the use of traditional breeds will reduce emissions.
mixed grazing systems incorporating cattle improve both livestock production and the conservation value of upland farming systems.

Mixed grazing systems incorporating cattle and improved pasture, and semi natural rough grazing, improve livestock productivity and numbers and species richness of birds and butterflies compared to systems based on sheep alone, and that it is possible to incorporate cattle grazing of semi natural pastures in summer without compromising livestock performance overall.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the management of semi-natural upland habitats and the impacts of livestock grazing on biodiversity.
the development and evaluation of sustainable livestock systems in relation to biodiversity and productivity.
identifying the best way to farm uplands sustainably in the face of a growing global demand for food and a need to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
mixed grazing systems incorporating semi natural pastures are beneficial to both biodiversity and livestock production.
mixed grazing systems incorporating cattle grazing and semi natural grasslands benefit both livestock production and biodiversity.
mixed grazing systems benefit both upland biodiversity and livestock production.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
mixed grazing systems are better than sheep systems for biodiversity and livestock production, but that the choice of cattle breed does not appear to be critical.
a mixed grazing system with cattle and sheep grazing improved pasture and semi natural grasslands, and a stocking density of 1.0-1.2 livestock units/ha, was best overall.

mixed grazing systems that include semi-natural rough grazing are the most sustainable option for upland farms, and that incorporating cattle into such systems can improve productivity and reduce emissions relative to sheep-only systems.
The main takeaway from our work is that
mixed grazing systems are a viable option for both farmers and conservationists to achieve their aims.
the incorporation of cattle into an upland farming systems can benefit both agricultural productivity and biodiversity.
it shows that it is possible to improve livestock production while also benefiting biodiversity, and that this can be done without resorting to conservation grazing with traditional breeds.
